analytic.title: New Schedulability Conditions for Real-Time Multiframe Tasks

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: The real-time multiframe task model first studied by Mok and Chen assumes that the computation times of a periodic task vary instance by instance. They have derived an utilization bound for verifying the schedulability of multiframe task sets. Their schedulability test has since been improved by other researchers. In this paper we use the information about the relative period ratios between tasks in a system to derive a new schedulability condition. By considering the smallest and the largest period values in a system, we can show that the RM schedulability bound can be improved significantly. This method also can be applied to other test methods studied earlier to improve the schedulability of real-time multiframe systems.

div.head: Introduction
div.p: Mok and Chen [10] first proposed a multiframe model for periodic real-time tasks in which the execution time of a task may vary from one instance to another but with a known pattern. One example is the transmission of MPEG-coded video frames. In MPEG coding standard, there are three types of video frames: I frame, P frame, and B frame. The maximum size of I frames is usually much bigger than those of P and B frames, and the frames are transmitted by a known pattern, such as "IBBPBBPBBIBBP ... ". It is too conservative if the maximum size of all types of frames is used as the worst-case transmission time for computing the schedulability of the tasks.

In a multiframe task set, each periodic task i is defined with parameters ((c i 0 , c i 1 , ... , c i Ni-1 ), p i ), where N i is the number of execution times of i , c i (j-1) mod Ni is the execution time of the jth job of i , and p i is the period of task i . The peak utilization factor of task i is max 0 j Ni-1 {c i j /p i }. The schedulability of real-time multiframe tasks using the Rate Monotonic (RM) fixed priority scheduling algorithm can be checked by totaling the peak utilization factors of tasks in the system. If the load (i.e. total peak utilization) of a system is less than or equal to a specific bound, the system is guaranteed to be schedulable.

An RM schedulability bound for multiframe systems was presented in [10]. In this paper, we present a period-ratio based method as a new RM schedulability bound for multiframe task systems. By using the ratio of the smallest and the largest period sizes in a system, we can show that the schedulability bound in [10] can be greatly improved. Moreover, the schedulability test for multiframe systems in [4] can also be improved by using our new bound. In our simulation study, the performance of the schedulability test in [4] could be improved by as much as 22% using our new bound.
The contributions of this paper are as follows:

1. We prove a new RM schedulability bound for multiframe task systems by considering the ratios of the smallest and the largest periods; 2. The new schedulability bound has been used to improve other multiframe schedulability test methods such as [4]. The remainder of this paper is as follows. In Section 2, we define the terminology for the proposed RM bound. Section 3 reviews well-known schedulability tests. Section 4 presents a RM schedulability bound according to the period ratio. A modified version of the schedulability test method proposed in [4] is shown in Section 5. A version of an incremental schedulability test is shown in Section 6. Section 7 provides the simulation results for the proposed schedulability test method. The paper is concluded in Section 8.

For analyzing the schedulability of multiframe tasks, Mok and Chen [10] have defined a special class of the multiframe task set, accumulatively monotonic (AM).

div.p: ), p i ) is said to be AM if its array of execution times is AM.

Intuitively an AM task is a task whose total execution time for contiguous L ( 1) frames is the largest among all contiguous L frames of the non-AM task. And the first frame of an AM task is the frame with the peak execution time. Any non-AM multiframe task can use a corresponding AM multiframe task for schedulability checking: if the AM task is schedulable in a task set, then the original non-AM task is schedulable [10]. For example, a non-AM task ((5, 2, 3), 10) or ((2, 5, 3), 10) can be tested as an AM task ((5, 3, 2), 10). A method is presented in [10] for finding the AM task from a non-AM task. Without loss of generality, we thus assume that all multiframe tasks are AM for the rest of this paper.

The critical instance of an AM multiframe task is the beginning of the period with its peak execution time requested simultaneously with the peak execution times of all higher priority tasks. It has been proved [10] that, for the preemptive fixed priority scheduling policy, an AM multiframe task is schedulable if it is schedulable in its critical instance.

div.head: Definition 4. Critical Jobs:
div.p: The critical jobs of an AM multiframe task set T = { 1 , 2 , ... , n } are jobs of tasks { 1 , 2 , ... , n-1 } (i.e. T-{ n }) with their periods beginning before t = p n and ending at or after t = p n . Example 3. Given T = { 1 = ((5, 3, 2), 10), 2 = ((3), 15)} is an AM multiframe task set. The critical job of T is the second job of 1 whose feasible period begins before p 2 (at t = 10) and ends after p 2 (at t = 20). Definition 5. [10] Extremely Utilizing Task Set: A task set is said to be extremely utilizing the processor if it is schedulable but no task in the set can increase its peak execution time without losing schedulability.

In this paper, we use a notation defined in [9] called the conditional bound (CB). CB(r, z) is a schedulability bound function of r and z. Given different r and z values, the CB function will have different values. In other words, the schedulability of a task set depends on these two task-set-derived parameters. Later in the paper we will show the details of the CB definition. Definition 6. Conditional Bound (CB(r, z)): An AM multiframe task set T is guaranteed to be RM schedulable if its total peak utilization is less than or equal to the bound CB(r, z), that is, U(T) CB(r, z) where r and z are two task-set-derived parameters.

The bound CB(r, z) is equal to the smallest total peak utilization among all extremely utilizing task sets with the same parameters r and z. As to be defined later in this paper, r = min 1 i n {r i } where r i = c i 0 /c i 1 if N i > 1 and r i = 1 if N i = 1 which is related to the ratio of peak utilizations and secondary utilizations, and z = max{p 1 /p n , r/(1+r)} which is related to period ratio.

div.head: Past work on schedulability tests and multiframe systems
div.p: When the value of N i of every periodic task i in a task set T = { 1 , 2 , ... , n } is equal to 1, T becomes a regular periodic task system. The utilization factor of task i is defined by u i = c i 0 /p i . If the total utilization of the system is less than or equal to some specified bound, the system is guaranteed to be schedulable.

Liu and Layland [6] have proposed the well-known RM bound (called the LL bound in this paper) for verifying the schedulability of periodic tasks. LL bound is n(2 1/n -1) where n is the number of periodic tasks in the system. Another schedulability bound proposed in [5] (called the Lauzac bound in this paper) considers the smallest period ratio in a system. Suppose z is the ratio of p 1 to p n in T. When the number of tasks in the system approaches infinity, the Lauzac bound is 2z-ln z-1; when the number of tasks in a system is n, the schedulability bound is 2z-1+(n-1)((1/z) 1/(n-1) -1). The LL bound is compared with the Lauzac bound as shown in Table 1. The gray area in Table 1 is close to LL bound. When z is close to 1, the Lauzac bound approaches 1 and is much better than the LL bound.

We have further improved the Lauzac bound in [9]. Our new schedulability bound is a function of z 1 and z 2 , where z 1 and z 2 are the smallest and largest period ratios in a system respectively. div.head: The Derivation of the CB Function
div.p: In this paper, a new multiframe schedulability bound is derived by considering the ratio between the smallest and the largest periods in a system. We first assume that p 1 > p n /2 in Section 4.1, and then the assumption is removed in Section 4.2.

div.head: CB for p 1 >p n /2
div.p: As in [9], our new bound is motivated by the observation that many jobs actually use more processor time than their fair share (by their peak utilizations) in RM schedules. Given task n with a deadline p n , other tasks' critical jobs may consume some time before p n even though their deadlines are later than p n . Hence, we define the gross utilization to reflect how much CPU time before p n is distributed among tasks. Definition 7. [9] Gross Utilization: For an AM task set T, let S be its RM execution schedule. The gross utilization of task i , denoted by y i , is defined by e i /p n where e i is the total time used by i during (0, p n ] in S. Assume J i,j is the jth job of i and with ready time less than p n . The gross utilization of job J i,j is defined by e i,j /p n where e i,j is the total time used by J i,j during ((j-1)p i , jp i ] in S. The gross utilization of task i is equal to the total gross utilization of jobs of i . Definition 8. [9] Excessive Utilization: For an AM task set T, the excessive utilization w i of task i is y i -u i 0 .

In S, every task i has two types of utilization u i 0 and y i . Since we assume all tasks are AM tasks, u i 0 is the peak utilization of i . y i is the gross utilization of i and depends on other tasks' parameters in the actual schedule. w i is the difference y i -u i 0 . (Note that for task n , the excessive utilization w n is always 0.) When the excessive utilization w i of all tasks is zero, no task will miss deadline even if the total utilization is 1.

div.head: Online admission control
div.p: Suppose there is a schedulable AM multiframe task set T = { 1 , 2 , ... , n }. When a new AM task = ((c 0 , c 1 , ... , c N-1 ), p) arrives at the system, we need to decide whether to admit the new task for execution. Let j be the maximum index of tasks in T whose period is less than the period of , and let T i be a set of merged tasks for 1 , 2 , ... , i (j i n). The basic idea of the online admission control is that if is schedulable after adding and merging with tasks in T j , the schedulability of tasks in T j+1 , ... , T n would be tested respectively after adding and merging with tasks in T j+1 , ... , T n . The new task is accepted to the system if all original tasks in the system remain schedulable after the admission; otherwise, the new task is rejected. The admission test for a new task arrival is shown in Algorithm 3.

div.head: Performance evaluation
div.p: We now compare the proposed CB and Kuo+CB schedulability tests with all multiframe schedulability tests reported in literature, including Mok and Chen [10], Han [1] and Kuo et al. [4].

div.head: Data set and measurement
div.p: The primary performance metric is the Guarantee Ratio. Let q be the number of task sets randomly generated and s the number of task sets guaranteed schedulable by a schedulability test. The Guarantee Ratio of the schedulability test is defined as s/q.

The task sets for performance evaluation are generated based on the benchmarks and systems reported in [2], [3], [8], [11]. The number of tasks per task set was randomly selected between 10 and 30. The number of fundamental frequencies is the number of tasks in the task set multiplied by a real number within the range [1/4, 1]. The data sets for the experiments are generated with a total peak utilization factor between 0.7 and 1.2. The experiments were started with each task set with a total peak utilization factor equal to 0.7, and were repeated for sets with the total peak utilization factor increasing in increments of 0.05 until 1.2 is reached. The peak utilization factor of each task is no more than 0.2 of the total peak utilization factor of its task set. Each task is assigned fundamental frequencies randomly, where the possibility of having k fundamental frequencies is (1/2) k-1 . The period of each task is derived by the product of all of its assigned fundamental frequencies. The size N i of the execution time array (c i ) is randomly chosen in the range (2,5). A total of 400 task sets are tested for each utilization factor. The task sets in the experiments are all schedulable based on the RM exact schedulability tests. Therefore, the guarantee ratio of an algorithm reflects the capability of the algorithm in identifying feasible task sets.

div.head: Experimental results
div.p: Fig. 2 shows the guarantee ratio of the CB test, Kuo+CB test and tests proposed by Mok and Chen [10], Han [1] and Kuo et al. [4] when r i is randomly chosen in the range (2,5). As shown in Fig. 2 When the range of r i changes from (2, 5) to (2, 10), the guarantee ratio of Kuo+CB test is again much better than all other test methods, as shown in Fig. 3. The guarantee ratio of Kuo+CB test is higher than that of Kuo's test by 22%, 19.5% and 16.5% when the CPU utilization is 1.1, 1.15 and 1.2 respectively. This is because when the CPU utilization is 1.1, 1.15 and 1.2 respectively, there are more than 57.25%, 73.25% and 88.75% task sets (among four hundred task sets) with a new CPU utilization > 0.8 after the task merge procedure. From Fig. 3, we can see that Mok's test has very low guarantee ratios while CB test has high guarantee ratios when the CPU utilization is > 0.8. Therefore, Kuo+CB test outperforms Kuo's test significantly.

div.head: Conclusions
div.p: In this paper, we present a new RM schedulability bound for real-time multiframe task systems. The proposed bound is a function of r which is related to the ratio of peak utilizations and secondary utilizations and z which is related to the ratio between the smallest and the largest periods in a system. By considering these parameters, a multiframe task system can be tested using a higher RM schedulability bound. This new schedulability bound can also be used to improve the schedulability test method in [4].
For future work, we plan to use this idea to look for other system parameters that may be used to improve the schedulability conditions of real-time systems.

The number of tasks tested in Kuo's test is much less than in other test methods. Between the two closed-form schedulability tests, CB test is much better than Mok's test when the CPU utilization ranges between 0.85 and 0.95. In particular, when the CPU utilization is 0.85, the guarantee ratio of CB test outperforms that of Mok's test by 42.5%.
